## Running recommenderlab on Azure

*Persistent Storage: Use a long-term storage solution. This can be either a database\
service such as Azure SQL Database, Cosmos DB, or file/blob storage using Azure\
Blob Storage.*

I used Azure blob storage to store my anime ratings and anime csv files. This was the easiest solution for directly reading a .csv into R.

![](images/clipboard-2344105951.png)

## Setting up a virtual machine

*Compute Resource: Use a compute service. This could be a virtual machine via Azure\
Virtual Machines, a containerized solution via Azure Container Instances or Azure\
Kubernetes Service (AKS), or a serverless function using Azure Functions.*

First, I set up a virtual machine, but there were no free storage options. I looked for B1/B2 storage options, but they were unavailable. Copilot told me that they were unavailable in my region, Eastern US, but also that they were available in my region, Eastern US. I eventually figured out that meant that they were currently fully in use (not region locked). I changed my region to Australia (after trying several other regions) and was able to use B2. However, this only offered 1 GB of memory.

![](images/clipboard-3103707915.png)

### Network security

*Network Security: Use an Azure Virtual Network (VNet) and configure Network\
Security Groups (NSGs) or private endpoints to ensure that only authorized users or\
applications can access your deployed resources.*

I ran the virtual machine in PowerShell and used my SSH network key to connect (key not pictured). Here, I also set the NSG to only allow my IP address.

### Run code

I installed packages: recommenderlab was not available, so I updated the version of R I was using so it could be installed.

![](images/clipboard-1908728937.png)

Then the VM crashed multiple times: it stopped installing R packages and wouldn't let me quit. I realized this was because the only storage I was able to get was 1 GB of RAM. I went back into Azure and upgraded to 8 GB.

This is all the code I ran (minus network security keys). I streamlined the code from project 4 so it just did what's required for this recommender. (Runtimes after the code).

```{r}
#ssh [user name]

R

library(AzureStor)

cont <- storage_container(
  "[Blob storage URL]",
  key = "[network key]"
)

storage_download(cont, "animeratings.csv", "anime.csv")
df <- read.csv("anime.csv")
head(df)


storage_download(cont, "animeratings.csv", "anime.csv", overwrite = TRUE)
df <- read.csv("anime.csv")
head(df)

#get item info
storage_download(cont, "anime.csv", "item_info.csv", overwrite = TRUE)
item_info <- read.csv("item_info.csv")
head(item_info)

#ubuntu will download tidyverse but won't run it as a package
#they have to be run individually
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(recommenderlab)

user_ratings <- df %>%
  filter(rating > -1)


#remove weird text from item info first
item_info$name <- gsub("&quot;", "", item_info$name)
item_info$name <- gsub("amp;", "", item_info$name)

#create other table

#join
user_item <- left_join(user_ratings, item_info |>
                         select(anime_id, name), by = "anime_id")

#remove the anime ID
user_item <- user_item |>
  select(user_id, rating, name)

#pivot wider
anime_table <- pivot_wider(
  data = user_item,
  names_from = name,
  values_from = rating
) 

library(tibble)

#create matrix

anime_matrix <- pivot_wider(
  data = user_item,
  names_from = name,
  values_from = rating
) |>
  column_to_rownames("user_id") |> 
  as.matrix()   


#create real ratings matrix
real_anime_matrix <- as(anime_matrix, "realRatingMatrix")

#min 15 ratings
real_anime_matrix20 <- real_anime_matrix[rowCounts(
  real_anime_matrix) > 15, ]



```

```{r}
set.seed(1122)
scheme <- evaluationScheme(real_anime_matrix20, 
                           method = "split", 
                           train = 0.8, 
                           #giving the model access to 15 ratings
                           #most users will have a few more than this
                           given = 15, 
                           #ratings are on a 1-10 scale
                           goodRating = 6)


set.seed(1122)
results_3 <- evaluate(scheme, method = "SVD", type = "ratings")

avg(results_3)

results_4 <- evaluate(scheme, 
                    method = "SVD",
                    type = "topNList", 
                    n = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40))

#check the results
avg(results_4)
```

I wasn't sure if Azure would run faster than my local machine, since they both have 8 GB of ram, but it did. The recommenders and runtimes:

![](images/clipboard-2015983209.png)

![](images/clipboard-2131840349.png)

![](images/clipboard-3242978022.png)

Runtime was about the same as the one I ran on my local machine. Azure took 3.97 seconds, and my local machine took 4.33. On the second algorithm, Azure took 4 seconds and my local machine also took about four seconds. My local machine:

![](images/clipboard-2863710971.png)

![](images/clipboard-3722202440.png)

After this, I decided to check UBCF, a more computationally-intensive algorithm, to see if it ran any faster in azure. It only took 3 minutes as opposed to 318 seconds (about 5.25 mins) to run.

```{r}

#create recommender
rec1 <- Recommender(getData(scheme, "train"), method = "UBCF")

#predictions - let's see the recommendations for these 6 users

pre <- predict(rec1, real_anime_matrix20[150:155], n = 5)
pre
as(pre, "list")


#check the accuracy 
results <- evaluate(scheme, method = "UBCF", type = "ratings")


avg(results)


results_2 <- evaluate(scheme, 
                    method = "UBCF",
                    type = "topNList", 
                    n = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40))

avg(results_2)
```

### Graph the comparison

Here's a comparison of the results of the two recommenders with a graph created in and downloaded from Azure.

```{r}

#extract performance metrics
metrics_svd  <- avg(results_4)  |>
  as.data.frame() |> 
  mutate(Method = "SVD",  N = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40))

metrics_ubcf <- avg(results_2) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(Method = "UBCF", N = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40))


plot_data_line <- bind_rows(metrics_svd, metrics_ubcf) |>
  select(Method, N, precision, recall) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(precision, recall), names_to = 
                 "Metric", values_to = "Value")

#graph
p_line <- ggplot(plot_data_line, aes(x = N, y = Value, color = Method, group = Method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~Metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Model Comparison: Precision and Recall @ N",
    x = "Number of Recommendations (N)",
    y = "Score",
    color = "Algorithm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")

# 4. Save the line graph to your VM
ggsave("model_comparison_line.png", plot = p_line, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)

# 5. Upload it directly to your Azure storage container
storage_upload(cont, "model_comparison_line.png", "model_comparison_line.png")
```

![](images/clipboard-1473220305.png)

### Conclusion

There was an upfront cost to using Azure, including figuring out the interface, setting up a virtual machine, and trying to get free computing solutions to work. Powershell is also less convenient to use than R Studio. I ended up configuring R twice and having to troubleshoot issues with computing after R crashed. I also had to save the exact code I needed to run in R studio and test it first because Powershell doesn't have the same user-friendly environment as R Studio. However, the amount of time saved on running a more intensive algorithm on a data set with almost a million ratings was significant. Based on this test, run with the entire data set, I can infer that for larger, deployable recommenders, cloud computing and dedicated RAM are necessary and helpful.
